title: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors
subtitle: An eigenvalue is a scalar λ such that Ax = λx — multiplying a vector by A just scales it, without changing its direction. That special vector is an eigenvector. Finding eigenvalues means solving the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0. Finding eigenvectors means substituting each eigenvalue back and solving the resulting homogeneous system.
learningOutcome: An eigenvalue is a scalar λ such that Ax = λx — multiplying a vector by A just scales it, without changing its direction. That special vector is an eigenvector. Finding eigenvalues means solving the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0. Finding eigenvectors means substituting each eigenvalue back and solving the resulting homogeneous system.

content.text: The eigenvalue equation Ax = λx can be rearranged to (A − λI)x = 0. This homogeneous system has non-trivial solutions only when the matrix (A − λI) is singular — that is, when its determinant is zero. So eigenvalues are the values of λ that satisfy det(A − λI) = 0.
Setting up and expanding that determinant gives you the characteristic polynomial p(λ). Its roots are the eigenvalues. For a 2×2 matrix you get a quadratic; for 3×3 you get a cubic.
-(λ+2)²(λ-4) = 0 λ + 2 = 0 → λ = -2 (repeated root, multiplicity 2) λ - 4 = 0 → λ = 4

Common mistake — When solving (A − λI)x = 0 for eigenvectors, students try to find a unique solution. But the whole point is that there's no unique solution — at least one component is free (that's what it means to be a null space vector). If you get x = 0 as the only solution, you made an arithmetic error somewhere in the eigenvalue step.

Eigenvalue questions are in Section B of the exam — they carry the most marks. 2019/2020 Q3 alone is worth over 20 marks covering eigenvalue theory, characteristic polynomials, properties, and Cayley-Hamilton.

topics.title: Finding Eigenvectors — One for Each Eigenvalue

subtopics.title: Finding Eigenvectors — One for Each Eigenvalue

content.text: Once you have eigenvalue λ, substitute it back into (A − λI)x = 0 and solve the homogeneous system. You get a relationship between the components of x — the eigenvector is any non-zero vector satisfying that relationship. Conventionally pick the simplest integer values.
Find eigenvectors for A = [[1,0],[2,3]] with λ₁=1 and λ₂=3
A - 1·I = [ 1-1 0 ] = [ 0 0 ] [ 2 3-1 ] [ 2 2 ] System: [ 0 0 ][ x₁ ] = [ 0 ] [ 2 2 ][ x₂ ] [ 0 ] Row 2: 2x₁ + 2x₂ = 0 → x₁ = -x₂ Row 1: 0x₁ + 0x₂ = 0 → always true (no new info) Let x₂ = 1 → x₁ = -1
Eigenvector for λ₁ = 1: x₁ = [−1, 1]ᵀ (or any scalar multiple)
A - 3·I = [ 1-3 0 ] = [ -2 0 ] [ 2 3-3 ] [ 2 0 ] System: [ -2 0 ][ x₁ ] = [ 0 ] [ 2 0 ][ x₂ ] [ 0 ] Row 1: -2x₁ + 0x₂ = 0 → x₁ = 0 Row 2: 2x₁ + 0x₂ = 0 → x₁ = 0 (same info) x₂ is free — let x₂ = 1
